disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation, is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, impulsivity, and difficulty inhibiting responses, with relatively fewer inattentive symptoms. Onset is typically in childhood, but functional impairment may become more evident or problematic later when environmental demands increase, such as in school, work, or complex social roles. The course is often chronic, though manifestations can change with age, with overt motor restlessness in children evolving into inner restlessness, impatience, and impulsive decision-making in adolescents and adults. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern across settings, and core deficits in inhibitory control and self-regulation rather than primarily mood or situationally driven behavioral issues.

narrative.personality: Alan is a meticulous, detail‑oriented planner who thrives on organized projects and structured routines, even if he sometimes over‑schedules himself and fixates on his hobbies.
narrative.stressor: Over the past two years, Alan has been trying to transition from odd jobs into a stable warehouse role, pushing himself to prove that he can handle full‑time responsibilities despite leaving high school early. He poured his energy into teaching himself inventory software and building elaborate planning systems at home, but when he began a trial period at a local warehouse, the fast pace, long shifts, and constant demands for on‑the‑spot decisions clashed with his need for tight structure and control. As the job expectations ramped up, he found it harder to match his careful planning with what supervisors described as the need to "be on your feet and just go," leading to repeated feedback that he seemed unable to settle into tasks, was disrupting the flow of work, and couldn't adapt to the warehouse's rhythm. After losing the trial position and noticing that his inability to stay settled was spilling over into his model building, home projects, and even family interactions, he became worried that something more than stress was going on and agreed, at his mother's urging, to seek psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t sit still long enough to do anything the way I plan it.”

narrative.personality: Irene is a reserved, highly organized woman who approaches daily life with disciplined routines, careful budgeting, and a quiet but competitive streak in social and intellectual activities.
narrative.stressor: After her divorce many years ago and eventual retirement from her community liaison role, Irene slowly rebuilt a structured life around her garden, chapel, and volunteer work, finding comfort in predictable routines and small, close‑knit groups. About a year and a half ago, several changes converged: her senior center expanded its programs, she took on more leadership in cooking workshops, and her long‑standing bridge group merged with a newer, more fast‑paced table that expected rapid play and constant table talk. The increased social demands, especially in group settings where conversations and decisions moved quickly, began to expose a longstanding tendency to jump in and take charge before others finished speaking, which now caused friction in classes and at the card table and left her feeling embarrassed and "out of step" with peers. When a visiting social worker gently pointed out that these longstanding behaviors seemed to be intensifying and were affecting her relationships and enjoyment of activities, Irene—already attentive to her health and functioning—agreed to a psychiatric referral to understand why she was suddenly having more difficulty holding back in group interactions.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep jumping in and answering people before they even finish what they’re saying, and it’s starting to cause problems in my groups.”

narrative.personality: Gregory is a driven, practical young man who channels his competitive energy into work, fitness, and community mentorship, preferring action‑oriented, hands‑on pursuits.
narrative.stressor: Gregory left college to focus on trucking and sales work, telling himself that if he worked harder and longer than everyone else, he could quickly move up to a logistics coordinator role. Over the past year and a half, his schedule intensified as he juggled long driving shifts, sales targets, gym time, and studying for his Class A CDL, leaving very little downtime and almost no slow, unstructured moments. In this high‑pressure, constantly moving lifestyle, his longstanding difficulty tolerating stillness and quiet became more pronounced: breaks, mandatory waiting periods, and even hanging out with friends in calm settings felt unbearable, driving him to seek out more stimulation and side activities in ways that started to interfere with safety at work, his study efforts, and his reliability with mentorship commitments. After a supervisor warned him that his inability to settle and "just sit" during mandatory rest periods could cost him his job and CDL prospects, and his mentor at the youth program suggested that his restlessness seemed beyond normal youthful energy, Gregory agreed to see a psychiatrist to figure out why he struggled so much with anything that wasn’t full‑throttle.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t handle just sitting still or doing anything low‑key—I always end up turning it into something loud or intense.”
